blocks.text: As רחם racham is named from mercy, so the bird that follows, חסידה hasida, or asida, as some write it with the aspiration dropped, is named from piety. I find a great many interpretations of this word. I. First, the Septuagint translators render it ἐρωδιόν [erōdion], and the Vulgate translator herodium or herodionem, that is, heron, in the Law and in verse nineteen of Psalm one hundred and three (one hundred and four in the Hebrew). Aquila too consistently has ἐρωδιόν [erōdion], as do Symmachus and Theodotion at Zach. V, 9. I also have two manuscript Arabic Psalters, one of which, in the place cited above, has الهيرودي [al-hīrūdī] alheiraudi, τὸν ἐρωδιόν [ton erōdion]. The Ethiopic likewise has ሄሮድዮስ፡ herodios. To the same I refer what stands in the Paris edition of the Psalms, البلشوم [al-balshūm] albalsum. For the bird بلشوم [balshūm] balsum, or بلشون [balshūn] balsun, also called مالك الحزين [mālik al-ḥazīn] malich alhazin, certainly seems to be the heron. This I gather from the descriptions of the Arabs, which run thus. Damir: البلشون هو مالك الحزين [al-balshūn huwa mālik al-ḥazīn] Abalsun is Malich alhazin. Giauhari: مالك [col. 322] الحزين هو طير الما [mālik al-ḥazīn huwa ṭayr al-māʾ] Malich alhazin is a water bird. Ibno Bari in his Marginal Notes: هو طير طويل العنق والرجلين [huwa ṭayr ṭawīl al-ʿunuq wa-l-rijlayn] It is a bird with a long neck and legs. Alkazuinius likewise: طير طويل الرقبة والرجلين يقال له بالفارسية بوتيما [ṭayr ṭawīl al-raqaba wa-l-rijlayn yuqāl lahu bi-l-fārisiyya būtīmā] A bird with a long neck and legs, which in Persian is called BUTHIMA. The same author, and Damir from Algiahid: من اعاجيب الدنيا امر مالك الحزين لانه لا يزال يقعد بقرب الما ومواضع نبعها من الانهار وغيرها فاذا انقصت حزن عليها ويبقي حزينا كييبا وربما ترك الشرب حتي يموت عطشا خوفا من زيادة نقصها بشرب منها [min aʿājīb al-dunyā amr mālik al-ḥazīn li-annahu lā yazālu yaqʿudu bi-qurb al-māʾ wa-mawāḍiʿ nabʿihā min al-anhār wa-ghayrihā fa-idhā anqaṣat ḥazina ʿalayhā wa-yabqā ḥazīnan kayīban wa-rubbamā taraka al-shurb ḥattā yamūta ʿaṭashan khawfan min ziyādat naqṣihā bi-shurbihi minhā] Among the wonders of the world is what they say of malich alhazin: that it always lives by the waters, whether of rivers or springing from elsewhere. When it sees them diminish, this torments it so that it remains sad and sorrowful, and sometimes abstains from drinking so long that it dies of thirst, lest they be diminished too much if it drinks from them. There follows in Damir a not dissimilar fiction about a kind of glow-worm, which the Arabs say shines by night, is winged, green and smooth, flits near rivers and feeds on the dust of the earth, but so sparingly and meagrely that it is never sated and sometimes dies of hunger, fearing the dust of the earth would run out if [III, 79] it ate its fill. These things were invented by the poets as types of the avaricious man, who denies himself what he has taken from others and cheats his own appetite. But truer is what Attaugides reports of the same bird in the book الامتناع والموانسة [al-imtināʿ wa-l-muwānasa] Of Antipathy and Sympathy: مالك الحزين ينشل الحيتان من الما فياكلها وهي طعامها ولا يحسن السباحة فان اخطاه الانتشال وجاع طرح نفسه علي شاطي البحر وفي بعض ضحضاحاته فاذا اجتمع اليه السمك الصغار اسرع في خطف ما استطاع منها [mālik al-ḥazīn yanshilu al-ḥītān min al-māʾ fa-yaʾkuluhā wa-hiya ṭaʿāmuhu wa-lā yuḥsinu al-sibāḥa fa-in akhṭaʾahu al-intishāl wa-jāʿa ṭaraḥa nafsahu ʿalā shāṭiʾ al-baḥr wa-fī baʿḍ ḍaḥḍāḥātihi fa-idhā ijtamaʿa ilayhi al-samak al-ṣighār asraʿa fī khaṭf mā istaṭāʿa minhā] Malich alhazin draws fish out of the waters, on which it feeds, and has them for its food, although it cannot swim. And when it is hungry and this fishing does not succeed, it throws itself from the seashore into the shallows, and from the little fish that approach it snatches with great haste whatever it can. Hence I infer that it is the heron, of which Oppian's paraphrast [Ixeut. book 2, ch. 8] says, in Gesner: They say that getting food from the waters was first discovered by herons, and that the rest learned it from them, since at the beginning all birds had one food. [col. 323] Then, since they gloried in this discovery and boasted that not even Neptune could compete with them in swimming, they lost this art through the god's anger, etc. Hence all other birds plunge into the water to catch fish; but herons, lacking the faculty of swimming, hunt standing on the shore. This mark is most certain, since among water birds there is no other that cannot swim. Here is another mark in Damir, though less explicit: وهو لا يحتاج الي تزواج الاسفاد [wa-huwa lā yaḥtāju ilā tazwāj al-isfād] It does not desire copulation and coition. Namely, because it does not mate without pain. The Philosopher, History, book 9, ch. 1: Τῶν δ’ ἐρωδιῶν ἐστι τρία γένη· ὅ τε πέλλος, καὶ ὁ λευκὸς, καὶ ὁ ἀστερίας καλούμενος. Τούτων ὁ πέλλος χαλεπῶς εὐνάζει τε, καὶ ὀχεύει. κράζει τε γὰρ, καὶ αἷμα, ὥς φασιν, ἀφίησιν ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὀχεύων. [Tōn d’ erōdiōn esti tria genē; ho te pellos, kai ho leukos, kai ho asterias kaloumenos. Toutōn ho pellos chalepōs eunazei te, kai ocheuei. krazei te gar, kai haima, hōs phasin, aphiēsin ek tōn ophthalmōn ocheuōn.] And again in ch. 18: Τῶν δ’ ἐρωδιῶν ὁ μὲν πέλλος, ὥσπερ εἴρηται, ὀχεύει μὲν χαλεπῶς. [Tōn d’ erōdiōn ho men pellos, hōsper eirētai, ocheuei men chalepōs.] Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 60: Of herons there are three kinds, leucon, asterias, pellos. These suffer distress in coition. The males indeed pour blood from their eyes as they cry out. Accordingly the Etymologicum, and Eustathius on Iliad κ, would have ἐρωδιὸν [erōdion] named παρὰ τὸ ἔαρ, vel ἔωρ, ὃ σημαίνει τὸ αἷμα, καὶ ἰδίειν τὸ ἱδροῦν. ἐν γὰρ ταῖς μίξεσιν (ὥς φασιν) ἡ ἐρωδιὸς αἷμα ἱδροῖ [para to ear, vel eōr, ho sēmainei to haima, kai idiein to hidroun. en gar tais mixesin (hōs phasin) hē erōdios haima hidroi], from ἔαρ [ear] or ἔωρ [eōr], which means blood, and ἰδίειν [idiein], which is to sweat. For the heron, as they say, sweats blood in coition. But I prefer to agree with those who say ἐρωδιὸς [erōdios] is as it were ἐλωδιὸς [elōdios], marsh bird: φιληδεῖ γὰρ τοῖς ἑλώδεσι τόποις [philēdei gar tois helōdesi topois], for it delights in marshy places. Now a third mark follows. The Muslim theologians permit eating the balsun, or malich alhazin; but, as the sons of the physicians assert, لحمه غليظ بارد [III, 80] يولد ادمان اكله البواسير [laḥmuhu ghalīẓ bārid yuwallidu idmān akalihi al-bawāsīr] Its flesh is coarse and cold, and the excrements from eating it produce haemorrhoids. This very thing Arnoldus de Villa-nova teaches about the heron, in Gesner, in these words: Whoever frequently suffers from haemorrhoids, especially throbbing ones, should above all beware, among other things, of cranes and agrones (that is, herons). Certainly, then, بلشوم [balshūm] balsum, or بلشون [balshūn] balsun, is the heron ^{(1)}, which from the fable we have related is called by another name مالك الحزين [mālik al-ḥazīn] malich alhazin, the sad waterer or sad drinker. For ملك [mlk] malch among the Arabs means, among other things, water. I note this here because the lexicographers have omitted the word بلشوم [balshūm] or بلشون [balshūn].
